lines: Melting ice takes in heat. So why does it happen all by itself?
A. The warm room forces it. B. It's secretly exothermic. C. Disorder goes up: entropy.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A says the warm room pours heat in.
Team B says it must release hidden energy.
Team C says it's about disorder, not just heat.
Year thirteen A-level chemistry: entropy, S. Ice is ordered; liquid water, more disordered.
Melting raises entropy by twenty-two joules per kelvin per mole.
Gibbs free energy: delta G equals delta H minus T delta S. Feasible when delta G is zero or negative.
Melting takes in six point oh one kilojoules per mole. Set delta G to zero, solve for T.
Six thousand and ten over twenty-two: two hundred and seventy-three kelvin. Zero degrees Celsius.
Above that, T delta S beats delta H, delta G goes negative, and ice melts.
Team A gets half a point: temperature multiplies the entropy term.
So it's C. Entropy and Gibbs free energy are on your A-level chemistry spec.
The catch? Freezing gives out heat, yet above zero degrees, water never freezes.
Exothermic isn't enough. Disorder gets a vote. Follow Full Marks.
Blood leaves your lungs full of oxygen. At rest, how much do your cells actually take out?
A. Nearly all of it. B. About a quarter. C. About half.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A says cells are greedy. Why send any back?
Team B says your body keeps a reserve.
Team C says split it: half out, half back.
Year twelve A-level biology: the oxygen dissociation curve.
In the lungs, oxygen partial pressure is high, so haemoglobin loads to about ninety-eight percent saturation.
In resting tissues, it only falls to about five kilopascals.
There, haemoglobin is still about three quarters saturated. So on average, your body takes about a quarter.
But that's the steep part of the S-shaped curve. A small drop in partial pressure releases much more oxygen.
Busy muscles make more carbon dioxide. Haemoglobin's affinity drops, the curve shifts right: the Bohr effect.
So it's B. Haemoglobin and the Bohr effect are on your A-level biology spec.
The catch? That's an average. Your heart muscle takes well over half, even at rest.
So a harder-working heart can't take much more. It needs more blood flow.
Biology with a built-in reserve? Follow Full Marks.
All eight billion people on Earth, in one alphabetical list. At most, how many checks to find one name?
A. About eight billion. B. Thirty-three. C. About ninety thousand.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A checks names one by one: up to eight billion.
Team B says halve the list every time.
Team C picks the square root. Ninety thousand sounds clever.
This is binary search, from A-level computer science.
Check the middle name. Is your target before it or after it?
Either way, one check throws away half the list.
Eight billion becomes four billion, then two billion, then one billion, and so on.
Two to the power thirty-three is about eight point six billion. So thirty-three halvings cover everyone.
A linear search could need eight billion checks. That's big O of n, against big O of log n.
So it's B: thirty-three checks, at most. Time complexity is on your A-level computer science spec.
The catch? It only works if the list is already sorted. Sorting eight billion names is the slow part.
Double the world to sixteen billion, and you need just one more check. Follow Full Marks.
Perfect weather. Farmers grow their biggest harvest ever. What happens to their total revenue?
A. It falls. B. It rises. C. It stays the same.
Comment your letter before the reveal.
Team A smells a trick question.
Team B says more to sell means more money.
Team C says prices drop, so it all evens out.
This is Year twelve A-level economics: price elasticity of demand.
A bumper harvest shifts supply to the right, so the price falls.
Food is a necessity. Cheaper bread doesn't make us eat much more: demand is price inelastic.
Say farmers usually sell a hundred units at three pounds: three hundred pounds.
The bumper crop is a hundred and ten units. To sell them, the price falls to two pounds.
Revenue: two hundred and twenty pounds. Ten percent more crop, over a quarter less revenue.
With inelastic demand, price and total revenue move in the same direction.
So it's A. Elasticity and total revenue are on your A-level economics spec.
The catch? For one farmer alone, a bumper crop is great. The price barely moves.
It only hurts when every farmer has one: the fallacy of composition.
Economics that sounds backwards? Follow Full Marks.
